bullets.text: ML is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence, focused on systems learning from data.
Learns patterns from data to make decisions or predictions, rather than fixed rules.
Models improve over time with more data without needing to be reprogrammed.
It's about teaching computers to learn from experience, similar to humans.
ML is ubiquitous: Netflix recommendations, spam filters, virtual assistants, fraud detection.
Its popularity is due to access to huge amounts of data.
Enabled by increased computational power, especially modern GPUs.
Driven by the development of sophisticated algorithms.
Most common type, trained using labeled data (input + correct output).
Model learns input-output relationships to predict outputs for new data.
Example: predicting house prices based on features and actual sale prices.
Problems are categorized as regression (continuous values) or classification (discrete labels).
Uses unlabeled data; the goal is to discover patterns, relationships, or structures on its own.
Common application: clustering, like grouping customers by buying behavior.
Also used for dimensionality reduction to simplify datasets with many features.
An agent learns by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback.
Adjusts its strategy based on rewards or penalties to maximize total reward.
Examples: training robots to walk, game-playing AI (AlphaGo), self-driving cars.
Data quality is crucial; noisy, biased, or incomplete data degrades performance.
Overfitting occurs when a model learns training data too well but fails on new data.
Ethical concerns are prominent, as biased data can lead to biased models with serious consequences.
ML requires understanding data, context, and the real-world impact of models.
